ATH / ATL.long:
ATH is all-time high, ATL all-time low: the highest and lowest prices an instrument has ever traded. Both are simple factual records, and both get loaded with meaning they do not carry.

The useful mechanical point is what an all-time high means for positioning. At a genuine ATH, nobody who bought the instrument is holding a loss — there is no trapped supply overhead waiting to sell into a recovery, because every previous buyer is in profit. That is a real structural difference from a price sitting below years of stacked entries, and it is why breakouts to new highs behave differently from breakouts within a range. The mirror holds at an ATL: nobody is underwater on a short.

The records are also relative to the data you have. An ATH on a chart that starts in 2017 is not an all-time anything.

Where people get fooled: treating an ATH as automatically expensive and an ATL as automatically cheap. Instruments in long uptrends spend much of their life at or near all-time highs — that is what an uptrend is — and instruments in terminal decline keep setting new lows all the way to nothing. The record says where price has been, not what it is worth.
ATH / ATL.usage: Generally quoted as a milestone; the mechanically interesting part is that at an all-time high no holder is trapped in a loss.

Alpha / beta.long:
Beta is the portion of a return explained by moving with the market; alpha is what is left after that is subtracted. A portfolio that rose because everything rose earned beta. A portfolio that rose more than its market exposure explains earned alpha — if the measurement was done honestly.

The distinction matters because beta is cheap and alpha is not. Broad market exposure costs a few basis points through an index fund, so any strategy charging more than that has to justify itself on the residual. Measuring the residual properly means comparing against the right benchmark at the right exposure level — a leveraged long position in a rising market produces large returns and no alpha at all, though it is routinely marketed as skill.

In trading slang the words drift from their statistical meaning: alpha becomes any edge or any useful information, and alpha decay becomes the observation that shared edges stop working.

Where people get fooled: mistaking beta for alpha during bull markets. Everyone holding risk looks skilled when risk pays, and the separation only becomes visible when the market stops carrying the return. Judging a track record without knowing its market exposure is judging nothing.
Alpha / beta.usage: Generally used to separate market-driven return from the residual; the residual is the only part that needs explaining.

Cope.long:
Cope is internet slang for a rationalisation offered after being wrong — the losing holder explaining why the loss does not count, the missed entry reframed as discipline, the thesis quietly rewritten to match the outcome.

Underneath the mockery sits a real and well-documented process. People reduce the discomfort of holding a belief that reality contradicted by adjusting the belief rather than accepting the error, and trading produces that discomfort on a schedule. The trading-specific forms are recognisable: a trade becomes an investment once it moves against you, a stop becomes a suggestion, a timeframe extends until the position is right, and a loss becomes tuition. Each reframing feels like perspective from the inside and functions as an excuse not to record the error.

The accusation is also thrown at correct analysis that happens to be unpopular, which makes it useless as an argument and only useful as self-diagnosis.

Where people get fooled: by their own version. Coping is invisible from inside because a rationalisation that felt like one would not work. The check is external and mechanical — what did the written plan say before the trade, and does the journal record what actually happened? A record made in advance cannot be renegotiated afterwards.
Cope.usage: Generally thrown as an accusation online; the useful application is checking your own post-loss explanations against what the plan said beforehand.
